The question of whether every startup needs a business plan is genuinely contested, with credible sources on both sides. Several sources argue strongly that a business plan is essential: [d4] (Investopedia) states that "a business plan is a fundamental document that any new business should have in place prior to beginning operations" and that "operating without a business plan usually is not a good idea," while [d8] asserts "every business needs a business plan no matter how large or small it begins," and [d5] claims "every startup needs a solid business plan serving as its blueprint for success regardless of its nature or size." [d1] and [d3] similarly frame a business plan as a critical step, especially for securing financing from banks and investors.

On the other hand, a significant body of evidence challenges this view. [d6] (Business Insider) argues directly that "a business plan isn't needed for every business," noting that if a startup is "aiming not to borrow money, a plan may not provide any advantage at all." [d9] (Insureon) explicitly states that startups are "generally not required" to have a business plan, though it can be helpful. [d10] reports that 70% of surveyed investors prefer pitch decks over business plans and that "most no longer consider business plans as necessary fundraising tools." [d11] (Harvard Business Review) describes the lean startup methodology as replacing the traditional business plan approach, with startups instead "searching for a business model" through testing and customer feedback rather than writing a formal plan.

In summary, whether a startup needs a business plan depends on its context: [d4] and [d8] make the case for universal necessity, while [d6], [d9], [d10], and [d11] present credible arguments that formal business plans are not always required, particularly for bootstrapped startups or those using lean or pitch-deck-based approaches.
